standard.title: Economic indicators
standard.description: how and why the economic indicators influence economic decision-making
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand the role of Australia's financial sector and its effect on economic decision-making by individuals, businesses and global markets (AC9HE9K01). They understand how economic decision-making involves the interdependence of consumers, businesses, the financial sector and government (AC9HE9K02). They can explain how economic decisions by one actor affect others across the system.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how and why economic indicators influence economic decision-making by governments, businesses and individuals in Australia.

nodes.label: What economic indicators are
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify key economic indicators and describe what each measures about the economy.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least three economic indicators (e.g. GDP growth rate, unemployment rate, inflation rate) and state what each measures.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and explain a range of economic indicators including GDP growth, unemployment trends, inflation rates, and sustainability indexes; describe what each measures and what it signals about economic conditions.
wider: Investigate composite indexes such as the OECD Better Life Index or the Genuine Progress Indicator and evaluate what they add to traditional economic indicators
Compare how different countries select and weight economic indicators, examining how political context shapes measurement priorities
Explore leading, lagging and coincident indicators and explain how their timing affects how decision-makers use them
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish what different indicators measure will conflate them when explaining how each influences decision-making. Without this foundation, later nodes on government response become vague ('the government responds to bad numbers') rather than specific.

response_modes.reason: Introduce indicators systematically — what is being measured, what unit, over what period, and what direction signals concern. Students commonly conflate GDP and employment, or confuse inflation with interest rates. A structured note-taking scaffold per indicator prevents this.
Build a reference set of indicators that students can draw on throughout the unit. Class-constructed reference cards or a shared table work well here.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of indicators is genuinely wide — sustainability indexes, composite wellbeing measures and non-traditional indicators offer rich cross-disciplinary connections and allow students to interrogate what 'economic health' means beyond conventional GDP metrics.
success_criteria: Names at least three distinct economic indicators and states what each measures
Distinguishes between indicators (e.g. can explain why unemployment and inflation measure different things)

nodes.label: Interpreting indicator data
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can read and interpret indicator data — identifying trends, describing what a change in direction signals, and using appropriate economic vocabulary.
nodes.minimum_width: Read a provided graph or table for one indicator; describe the trend and state what a rise or fall signals.
nodes.typical_width: Interpret data for multiple indicators across a time period; describe trends, identify turning points, and use terms such as economic growth, recession, inflation, unemployment rate accurately.
wider: Analyse a period of economic volatility (e.g. GFC, COVID-19) using multiple indicator datasets to explain what happened and in what sequence
Compare Australian indicator trends with those of a trading partner to identify divergence and consider its implications
Evaluate the limitations of a specific indicator — what it misses, who it undercounts, or what it obscures
nodes.hinge_reason: The rest of the descriptor requires students to explain how indicators *influence* decisions — this is only possible if they can read what the indicators are saying. Students who cannot interpret a trend cannot explain why a government might respond.

response_modes.reason: Practise reading graphs of different indicators with varied time periods. Common errors include misreading rate-of-change (confusing a slowing growth rate with a decline), or misinterpreting unemployment — knowing fluency here prevents errors in later analysis.
Expose students to data from different economic events and time periods so they can apply interpretation skills across varied contexts rather than pattern-matching to a single example.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Multiple economic events (GFC, COVID, post-COVID inflation) and the ability to compare international data offer rich real-world application. Students who can interpret across contexts develop genuine economic literacy.
success_criteria: Correctly describes the trend shown in a provided indicator dataset (rising, falling, stable, volatile)
Uses at least one specific economic term accurately when describing what the trend signals

nodes.label: Government economic objectives
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can name and explain the Australian Government's key economic objectives and connect each to one or more indicators that track progress toward it.
nodes.minimum_width: Name at least two government economic objectives (e.g. economic growth, full employment, price stability) and identify which indicator tracks each.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the Australian Government's main economic objectives — economic growth, full employment and price stability — and explain why each matters for living standards; connect each objective to its corresponding indicator(s).
wider: Investigate how environmental sustainability or wellbeing has been framed as a policy objective and which indicators governments are beginning to use to track it
Compare Australia's stated economic objectives with those of a different country and examine whether the same indicators are used
Examine how objectives can conflict (e.g. low unemployment can drive inflation) and how governments balance competing indicators
nodes.hinge_reason: Without understanding that indicators are proxies for objectives — that GDP is tracked because growth is a goal — students cannot explain *why* indicators matter to decision-making. They will describe reaction without understanding rationale.

response_modes.reason: Help students build the explicit connection: objective → what it means → why it matters → which indicator tracks it → what direction signals concern. This logic chain is the scaffold for the integration node.

success_criteria: Names at least two government economic objectives and explains why each matters for Australians
Correctly matches each objective to the indicator(s) used to track it

nodes.label: How indicators prompt government response
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how changes in specific indicators trigger or justify government economic decisions, using examples of actual or hypothetical government responses.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one example of a government response to a change in an economic indicator, explaining the connection between the indicator movement and the decision.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how the Australian Government may intervene in response to emerging economic issues or changes in indicators — such as responding to declining GDP with fiscal stimulus, or to rising inflation with interest rate signals — with reference to economic objectives.
wider: Analyse a specific historical case of government intervention (e.g. fiscal stimulus during GFC, COVID-19 JobKeeper) and evaluate whether the indicator signal justified the response
Investigate how international organisations (IMF, World Bank) use economic indicators to issue recommendations to governments and assess whether governments follow them
Examine the role of the Reserve Bank of Australia in interpreting inflation data and adjusting the cash rate, tracing the decision chain from indicator to policy

response_modes.reason: Use multiple real-world examples of government response across different indicator triggers so students can generalise the mechanism rather than memorise one case.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Real-world case studies of fiscal and monetary policy responses are rich, varied and widely available. Students who analyse multiple cases develop transferable reasoning about how indicator reading translates into policy — a genuine economic literacy outcome.
success_criteria: Explains a government decision with reference to a specific indicator change that preceded it
Names the economic objective the response was intended to serve

nodes.label: Indicators and individual/business decision-making
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how economic indicators influence decision-making beyond government — by businesses and individuals — and describe the logic of these responses.
nodes.minimum_width: Give one example of how an economic indicator (e.g. rising unemployment or inflation) affects a decision made by a business or individual consumer.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how indicators such as employment statistics, inflation rates and GDP growth influence decision-making by businesses (e.g. investment, hiring, pricing) and individuals (e.g. spending, saving, borrowing), and connect these to the broader economic picture.
wider: Investigate how consumer confidence surveys (a leading indicator) influence business investment decisions and explain the transmission mechanism
Analyse how a small business owner in a specific sector would interpret a suite of current indicators to make a decision about expansion or staffing
Compare how high-income and low-income households respond differently to the same indicator signal (e.g. rising interest rates) and examine equity implications

response_modes.reason: This node brings together indicator knowledge, government objectives and real-world actors into the full scope of the descriptor — how and why indicators influence economic decision-making across all actors. It synthesises the prior nodes.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Extending to business and household decision-making opens up genuinely varied real-world contexts — sector comparisons, income distribution, small business vs corporate responses. These widen economic literacy into students' lived experience.
success_criteria: Gives a specific example of how an indicator influences a decision by a non-government actor (business or individual)
Explains the reasoning behind the decision — why this indicator matters to this actor
